questions.title: technology
questions.passage: Few innovations have reshaped the classroom as swiftly as artificial intelligence. Advocates argue that students should embrace AI tools wholeheartedly, and their reasoning is compelling. A well-designed chatbot can clarify a baffling concept in seconds, generate practice questions tailored to a learner's weaknesses, and offer feedback at any hour without a hint of impatience. Therefore, for those who lack access to private tutors, such technology can be a remarkable equalizer. Nevertheless, an uncritical dependence on these tools carries genuine risks. When learners outsource every difficult task to a machine, they may never cultivate the perseverance and analytical thinking that authentic understanding demands. Moreover, AI systems occasionally generate confident yet inaccurate answers, and a student who cannot evaluate such claims is easily misled. Critics therefore warn that convenience can quietly erode intellectual independence. However, abandoning these tools altogether would be equally shortsighted, for they are becoming inseparable from modern life. The wisest course, then, is balance. Students ought to treat AI as a capable assistant rather than a substitute for their own effort, verifying its output and reserving the hardest thinking for themselves.

When the sun is low in the early morning or late afternoon, the light is soft and warm. A photo taken at these times often looks gentle and pleasing to the eye. Strong midday light, on the other hand, can create hard shadows on a person's face. Where you stand also makes a big difference to your final picture. If you move a little to the side, a messy background can disappear from view. Many beginners forget to hold the camera still, so their photos come out blurry. A simple trick is to keep your arms close to your body for support. With a little practice, anyone can learn to capture a clear and beautiful moment. In the end, patience and a good eye matter more than an expensive camera.

questions.title: healthy habits
questions.passage: Building healthy habits does not have to be hard or expensive. The first step is to drink enough water during the day, because our bodies need it to stay strong and clear. Many young people forget to eat breakfast, but a simple meal in the morning gives them energy for class. Moving the body is also important, so a short walk after dinner can help a lot. Sleep matters just as much as food and exercise. When students go to bed at the same time each night, they wake up feeling fresh and ready to learn. It also helps to spend less time staring at a phone before sleep. Eating fruit and vegetables every day keeps the body clean inside. None of these habits will change a life in one day. The real secret is to repeat small good choices until they feel normal and easy.

questions.title: robots
questions.passage: Some people worry that robots will take away all of our jobs in the future. I believe this fear is too strong, and that robots can actually help us instead. In factories, robots can lift heavy boxes that would hurt a human worker's back. In hospitals, they can carry tools quickly so that nurses have more time to care for patients. Robots are good at doing the same task again and again without getting tired or bored. However, they cannot smile at a sad child or make a hard choice based on feelings. This means humans are still needed for jobs that require kindness and clear thinking. Of course, we must learn new skills as machines become more common. If we use robots as helpers rather than replacements, both people and machines can do their best work. The future does not have to be a fight between humans and robots.

questions.title: forests
questions.passage: Students from Greenhill School spent last weekend planting young trees on a hill outside their town. The project was started after the class learned that the area had lost many trees to a fire three years ago. With help from local park workers, more than forty students dug holes and placed small trees into the ground. Each student also promised to return once a month to water the trees and check on them. Their teacher said the goal was to bring birds and small animals back to the bare hillside. A park worker explained that healthy forests also keep the soil in place and clean the air for everyone. The children were tired by the end of the day, but they felt proud of what they had done. The school now hopes that other classes will join the project next year. If the plan works, the green hill may once again be full of life.
